title.en: From the Rulers to the Ruled: Types of Governments

text.en: A class needs a committee to manage everyday tasks. One student says the teacher should choose, another says whoever is strongest, a third says everyone should vote. The class starts arguing. They have just discovered the main question of this chapter: who should rule, and how should they be chosen? Different countries answer in different ways.

Government plays an important role in our lives. It makes rules, which is the legislative function, carries them out, the executive function, and settles disputes, the judicial function. Governments differ in who or what gives them authority, what their parts are and what they do, and what goals they pursue.
Democracy is the most popular form of government in the modern world. It rests on ideas such as equality, freedom and universal adult franchise, the right of every adult citizen to vote, whatever their wealth, gender or religion. Freedom in democracy means citizens can make their own choices and express their opinions, as long as they do not harm others' rights. An independent judiciary protects fundamental rights and ensures that laws are followed by citizens and by the government itself. Elections are held at regular, fixed intervals. In ancient times too there were forms of democracy. In some Greek city-states free men could vote, but women, workers and slaves could not. In India, ancient sanghas and village councils used assemblies.
In a direct democracy, people take decisions themselves, as the class might do. In a representative democracy, people elect representatives to make laws for them. In a parliamentary system the people elect the legislature, and the executive, the prime minister and ministers, comes from the legislature and answers to it, as in India. In a presidential system the people elect both the legislature and the president separately. A country can also be federal, sharing power between a national government and state governments, as India does. The States are still governed by a larger national government, the Union Government of India.
In an absolute monarchy the king or queen has complete control over making laws, enforcing them and judging disputes, and the position passes from one generation to the next within the royal family. In a constitutional monarchy the monarch is the head of state but has only nominal power, and the real power of the executive lies with an elected prime minister. In many parts of India the power of the raja was neither absolute nor beyond question. The raja's highest duty was the welfare of his people, and a story tells of King Chandrapida who wanted a temple but the cobbler's hut stood in the way; the king respected the law and did not take it by force. Rulers still depended on a council of ministers and a network of officials.
A theocracy is a government ruled by religious law and religious leaders. An oligarchy is rule by a small group, such as the aristocratic families who ruled some places in ancient Greece. A dictatorship is rule by one person or a small group who hold all power and do not allow people to question them. Dictators often control the press, punish opponents, and set rules for ordinary life. In the 20th century some dictators, convinced of the superiority of their people, caused great suffering, as in Nazi Germany or under Idi Amin in Uganda. Cartoons are a way political commentators comment on rulers and governments.
In a democracy the ideals of the government should focus on the well-being of all. But democracies also face hurdles: money and power, misinformation and low participation. As individuals and as a society we must stay vigilant, vote wisely, ask questions and protect equal rights.

problem.en: Match each description with a type of government: one family, power passes by birth; a prime minister who answers to the legislature; all power in one person.

text.en: Power by birth in one family is a monarchy.
A prime minister answerable to the legislature is a parliamentary democracy.
All power in one person is a dictatorship.

requiredIdeas.en: In democracy people choose and can change rulers.
In dictatorship one person holds power without checks.
Democracy protects rights through an independent judiciary.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking all democracies are the same.

points.en: Governments make, carry out and judge laws.
Democracy is based on equality, freedom and universal adult franchise.
Other forms include monarchy, theocracy, oligarchy and dictatorship.
